name: Burgruine Thaur
kurzbeschreibung: The Burgruine Thaur and the Romedikirchl near Hall in Tirol: once a 12th-century stronghold of the Counts of Andechs, hermitage of St. Romedius, and open-air stage.
beschreibung:
Overview

The steeped-in-history Burgruine Thaur rises on a steeply falling, forested rocky outcrop of the Nordkette at an elevation of approximately 820 metres above the traditional vegetable-growing village of Thaur near Hall in Tirol. Together with the immediately adjacent, picturesque Romedikirchl, this historic ensemble constitutes one of the most charming cultural heritage sites in the Inn Valley. Where powerful counts and provincial judges once ruled over the central Inntal, day-trippers, hikers, and theatre lovers now enjoy a peaceful oasis with glorious panoramic views stretching across the entire Inn Valley, the historic salt town of Hall, and the provincial capital of Innsbruck.

History & Romedikirchl

The construction of the fortified stronghold dates back to the 12th century: the powerful Grafen von Andechs built the castle as a strategic administrative seat and court for the Landgericht Thaur; it was first documented around 1220. Following the extinction of the Andechs dynasty, the fortress passed into the possession of the Counts of Tyrol. In 1525, during the German Peasants' War, the fortress was besieged by rebellious peasants. A devastating fire in 1536 heralded the decline of the castle, and its ultimate destruction was sealed by the severe 1670 Inntal earthquake, whose epicentre lay in the Hall region. Directly below the main castle stands the prominent Romedikirchl (dedicated to St. Peter and St. Romedius): it traces its origin to the hermitage of Saint Romedius, a 4th/5th-century nobleman who according to legend lived as an anchorite on the Thaur castle rock and rode a bear to visit the bishop in Trent. The present Baroque pilgrimage church was erected from 1648 onwards and charms visitors with delicate stucco work and an altar painting depicting the hermit. In the 20th and 21st centuries, the ruins were carefully consolidated by the dedicated local castle and culture association; today, the castle courtyard serves as an atmospheric open-air stage for the renowned Thaurer Schlossspiele.

Visit & Getting There

The outdoor grounds of the Burgruine Thaur and the church precinct are freely accessible year-round and free of charge. The Romedikirche is open during the daytime for prayer and sightseeing. Access on foot: From Thaur village centre (e.g. the village square or parish church), a scenic signposted Stations of the Cross path leads up to the ruin in a leisurely 25 to 35-minute walk. Alternatively, a paved mountain road leads up to the hikers' car park below the Romedikirchl. By public transport: S-Bahn Tirol trains or bus routes 501/502 from Innsbruck Hauptbahnhof to the Thaur Volksschule or Mitte bus stop, and then uphill on foot. By car: From Hall in Tirol or Innsbruck along the D?rferstra?e (L321) to Thaur, following the signs to the Romedikirchl parking area (paid parking with limited spaces).

Tips

The path from the hikers' car park up to the Romedikirchl and into the inner courtyard of the castle ruins is surfaced with wide gravel and, with a bit of pushing effort, is manageable with all-terrain prams. From the viewing platforms along the ancient defensive walls, you can enjoy a fantastic view looking down over the historic rooftops of Hall in Tirol and the course of the Inn River. In summer, culture enthusiasts should book tickets early for the theatrical performances of the Thaurer Schlossspiele staged in the illuminated castle courtyard.
